cards.shape: Algeria is the biggest country in Africa (it took the title from Sudan when South Sudan split off in 2011), and almost all of that size is Sahara reaching far south of the narrow, populated Mediterranean coast. France ruled Algeria from 1830 and treated it as part of France itself rather than as an ordinary colony, so it ran the desert to the south from Algiers and kept extending Algeria's territory deep into the Sahara instead of handing it to its neighboring colonies. At independence in 1962, France tried to keep the Sahara, where it had found oil and gas and was testing nuclear bombs, but in the end it all went to Algeria, and Morocco's claim to part of the western desert led to a brief border war in 1963. The name comes from the capital, Algiers, from the Arabic al-Jaza'ir, "the islands," after small islands off its harbor.
facts: Rock paintings at Tassili n'Ajjer show giraffes and herds of cattle — from thousands of years ago, when the Sahara was green.
The largest country in Africa by area — over 80% of it is Sahara.
Won independence from France in 1962 after an eight-year war.
One of the world's big natural-gas exporters, piped under the Mediterranean to Spain and Italy.

cards.shape: Egypt looks like a near-square box of ruler-straight lines, but almost everyone lives on a thin green ribbon inside it: roughly 95% of Egyptians live along the Nile and its delta, on about 5% of the land. The straight lines are colonial-era deals across empty desert: the southern border with Sudan follows the 22nd parallel, set by Britain and Egypt in 1899, and the western border with Libya roughly follows the 25th meridian, agreed between Egypt and Italy in 1925. A later administrative line in the south is why Egypt and Sudan both claim the Halaib Triangle on the Red Sea, while the small Bir Tawil next to it is claimed by neither. The triangle across the Suez Canal is the Sinai Peninsula, which is in Asia, making Egypt a two-continent country; Israel occupied it in 1967 and returned it in 1982 after the 1979 peace treaty.
facts: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
About 95% of Egyptians live along the Nile, on roughly 5% of the land.
The Great Pyramid was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for about 3,800 years.
The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, links the Mediterranean to the Red Sea.

cards.shape: Libya is a big block of mostly Sahara made from three historic regions that were never really one place: Tripolitania in the west around Tripoli, Cyrenaica in the east around Benghazi, and the Fezzan in the southwestern desert, with hundreds of kilometers of empty coast and desert between the first two. Italy seized them from the Ottoman Empire in 1911-12 and in 1934 joined them into one colony, reviving "Libya," the ancient Greek name for North Africa west of Egypt. That east-west split still shows: the country had rival governments in Tripoli and the east after the 2011 revolution. The straight southern border with Chad was fought over too: Libya occupied the Aouzou Strip on the Chad side in 1973, citing an unratified 1935 French-Italian treaty, and the International Court of Justice gave it back to Chad in 1994.
facts: The Great Man-Made River pumps ancient groundwater from under the Sahara to coastal cities — one of the biggest water projects on Earth.
For 90 years Libya held the record for the hottest temperature ever (58 °C, 1922) — until it was thrown out as a measuring error in 2012.
Has the largest proven oil reserves in Africa.
More than 90% of the country is desert.

cards.shape: Whether Morocco ends at a short southern border or runs far down the Atlantic coast depends on whose map you look at, because the long territory below it, Western Sahara, is disputed. It was the colony of Spanish Sahara until Spain pulled out in 1975-76; in November 1975 Morocco sent some 350,000 civilians across the border in the "Green March" and split the territory with Mauritania; Mauritania gave up its share in 1979, and Morocco now controls most of it behind a long sand wall, while the Polisario Front, backed by Algeria, claims it as an independent state. Spain also still holds two small cities on Morocco's north coast, Ceuta and Melilla. The name "Morocco" comes from the city of Marrakesh, while in Arabic the country is al-Maghrib, "the west," since it was the far western end of the Arab world.
facts: The University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, founded in 859 by a woman, Fatima al-Fihri, is often called the world's oldest operating university.
Only about 14 km of water — the Strait of Gibraltar — separates Morocco from Spain.
Spain still holds two cities on Morocco's coast: Ceuta and Melilla.
Chefchaouen, in the Rif Mountains, is famous for its blue-painted streets.

cards.shape: Sudan used to be Africa's biggest country until 2011, when its south broke away as South Sudan, taking about a quarter of its land; what's left is still roughly three times South Sudan's size. Britain ran the country jointly with Egypt from 1899 and governed the mostly Arabic-speaking Muslim north and the largely Christian and traditional-religion south almost as separate territories, then handed it over as one country at independence in 1956. The south fought the government in Khartoum in two long civil wars, and a 2005 peace deal promised a referendum in which southerners voted almost unanimously to leave; the border, including the oil-rich Abyei area, is still partly disputed. The name comes from the Arabic bilad al-sudan, "land of the Black people," an old term for the whole belt of Africa south of the Sahara.
facts: Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt — about 200, built by the Nubian kingdoms of Kush and Meroë.
The Blue Nile and White Nile meet at Khartoum.
Until South Sudan split off in 2011, Sudan was the largest country in Africa.
Supplies most of the world's gum arabic, used in soft drinks and sweets.

cards.shape: Tunisia is the small one squeezed between Algeria and Libya, a corner of Africa that juts toward Sicily, and its outline is one of the oldest on the continent. This was the heartland of Carthage, then the Roman province of "Africa," which eventually gave the whole continent its name, and later the medieval region of Ifriqiya; by Ottoman times it was the largely self-governing beylik of Tunis, covering most of what is now Tunisia. When France took over in 1881 it made Tunisia a protectorate and left the bey on his throne, instead of folding it into the much bigger French Algeria next door, so it came out of colonial rule in 1956 as its own country. The name comes from the capital, Tunis.
facts: Star Wars filmed Luke Skywalker's home planet here — “Tatooine” is named after the Tunisian town of Tataouine.
The ruins of ancient Carthage, Rome's great rival, are in a suburb of Tunis.
The Arab Spring began here in December 2010.
The northernmost point of Africa is in Tunisia.

cards.shape: Benin is a narrow country running north from a short coast between Togo and Nigeria, because France built it outward from the coastal kingdom of Dahomey, which it conquered in the 1890s, pushing north until it reached the Niger River, which forms part of its border with Niger. It was called Dahomey until 1975, when the Marxist government renamed it after the Bight of Benin, the bay it sits on, a name that didn't favor the southern Fon kingdom over other groups. The famous Kingdom of Benin, with its bronzes, was not here at all but in today's Nigeria, around Benin City.
facts: Vodun (voodoo) originated here, and January 10 is a national Vodun holiday.
The Kingdom of Dahomey had an all-female army regiment — the inspiration for the film The Woman King.
Ganvié is a town of about 20,000 people built on stilts in a lake.
Its official capital is Porto-Novo, but the government sits in Cotonou.

cards.shape: Burkina Faso was called Upper Volta until 1984, because the Black, White and Red Volta rivers that flow south into Ghana begin here. France actually abolished the colony in 1932 and split it among Côte d'Ivoire, French Sudan (now Mali) and Niger, then put it back together in 1947 with roughly the same borders. In 1984 the revolutionary leader Thomas Sankara renamed it Burkina Faso, usually translated as "land of upright people", mixing a word from Mooré and one from Dyula, two of the country's main languages.
facts: Its architect Francis Kéré became the first African to win the Pritzker Prize, architecture's top award, in 2022.
The name means roughly “land of upright people”. It was called Upper Volta until 1984.
Ouagadougou hosts FESPACO, Africa's biggest film festival.

cards.shape: Cabo Verde is a group of ten islands about 570 km off Senegal at the nearest point, and its name, "green cape", comes not from the islands, which are mostly dry, but from Cap-Vert, the green headland near Dakar on the mainland that is the westernmost point of Africa. The islands were uninhabited when the Portuguese arrived around 1460, and became a hub of the Atlantic slave trade; most Cape Verdeans descend from enslaved West Africans mixed with Portuguese settlers. It won independence from Portugal in 1975 through the same movement as Guinea-Bissau, and the two were meant to unite until a 1980 coup in Bissau. Since 2013 it asks to be called Cabo Verde in every language instead of Cape Verde.
facts: On Fogo island people live and grow wine inside the crater of an active volcano — it last erupted in 2014.
An archipelago of 10 volcanic islands about 570 km off Senegal; uninhabited until the Portuguese arrived in the 1460s.
Home of morna music, made famous by the “barefoot diva” Cesária Évora.

cards.shape: European sailors named stretches of this coast after what they bought there, so from west to east you had the Grain Coast (Liberia, for melegueta pepper), the Ivory Coast, the Gold Coast (now Ghana) and the Slave Coast. The French kept the old trade name for their colony, and since 1985 the government has asked that it be called Côte d'Ivoire in every language rather than translated. Its tidy, squarish shape hides a quirk: in 1932 France broke up its neighbor Upper Volta (now Burkina Faso) and handed a large part of it to Côte d'Ivoire, until Upper Volta was put back together in 1947.
facts: In 2005 football star Didier Drogba knelt on live TV and begged both sides of the civil war to lay down their weapons — a ceasefire followed within a week.
The world's largest cocoa producer — around 40% of the global crop.
The government asks to be called Côte d'Ivoire in every language, not “Ivory Coast”.
Yamoussoukro's Basilica of Our Lady of Peace is one of the largest churches in the world.

cards.shape: The Gambia is a thin strip, mostly 20 to 50 km wide, that follows the Gambia River nearly 480 km inland, with Senegal wrapped around it on three sides. In the 1800s Britain held the river and its trading posts while France took the land all around it, and an 1889 Anglo-French deal fixed the border about 10 km from each bank. (The story that the border was set by cannon-shot range from the river is a legend.) The two countries tried a merger, the Senegambia Confederation, in 1982, but it broke up in 1989, partly because Gambians didn't want to be absorbed by their much bigger French-speaking neighbor.
facts: The smallest country on mainland Africa: a thin strip along the Gambia River, surrounded by Senegal except at the coast.
Legend says its borders were set by how far a British gunboat's cannon could fire from the river.
Kunta Kinteh Island in the Gambia River is tied to the slave trade and to Alex Haley's book Roots.

cards.shape: Ghana is named after the ancient Ghana Empire, which wasn't here at all but several hundred kilometers to the northwest, in today's Mauritania and Mali; the name was adopted at independence in 1957, when Ghana became the first sub-Saharan African colony to break free, and the British colony had been called the Gold Coast. Its eastern strip was part of German Togoland, which Britain and France seized in 1914 and split between them; in a 1956 vote the British western part chose to join Ghana, while the French part became Togo. The huge lake down the middle is Lake Volta, the world's largest artificial lake by surface area, created by the Akosombo Dam in the 1960s.
facts: Ghanaian “fantasy coffins” are carved in the shape of what the person loved — a fish, a plane, a Coke bottle.
In 1957 Ghana became the first sub-Saharan African colony to win independence, led by Kwame Nkrumah.
Lake Volta is the largest artificial reservoir in the world by surface area.
The Equator and Prime Meridian cross in the Gulf of Guinea, south of Ghana.

cards.shape: Guinea curves like a boomerang, from its short Atlantic coast up over the top of Sierra Leone and Liberia and then down their eastern side. Britain and the American-founded Liberia held those two coastal pockets, while France pushed in behind them in the late 1800s, joining its coastal colony to the Fouta Djallon highlands and the upper Niger, which rises in Guinea, so French Guinea ended up wrapped around them. It is one of three "Guineas" on this coast (an old European name for the whole region), so it is often called Guinea-Conakry after its capital; in 1958 it was the only French colony to vote no in de Gaulle's referendum and became independent at once.
facts: Called the “water tower of West Africa”: the Niger, Senegal and Gambia rivers all start here.
Has the world's largest reserves of bauxite, the ore of aluminium.
Mount Nimba is home to a rare toad that gives birth to live young instead of laying eggs.

cards.shape: Guinea-Bissau is a small, ragged wedge of coast and river mouths squeezed between Senegal and Guinea, with the Bijagós islands scattered offshore. It is what was left of Portugal's trading posts on this coast, some dating to the 1500s, after an 1886 deal with France in which Portugal gave up the Casamance region to the north (now southern Senegal) and the borders were fixed around it. It was Portuguese Guinea until it won independence in a war that ended in 1974, and it adds its capital to its name to tell it apart from its bigger French-speaking neighbor Guinea. The same liberation movement also fought for Cabo Verde, and the two were meant to unite until a 1980 coup in Bissau ended the plan.
facts: In the Bijagós islands, hippos swim in the sea between islands.
The Bijagós Archipelago is a cluster of about 88 islands, a UNESCO biosphere reserve.
Cashew nuts make up the vast majority of its exports.

cards.shape: Liberia's name means "land of liberty": it was founded in 1822 by the American Colonization Society as a home for freed Black Americans, its capital Monrovia is named after US President James Monroe, and its flag copies the Stars and Stripes. It declared independence in 1847 and was never a European colony, but it was squeezed by its neighbors, losing land along the coast to British Sierra Leone in the 1880s and inland territory to French Guinea and Côte d'Ivoire in treaties of 1892 and 1907. That is why it ended up as a fairly shallow strip along the coast, longer than it is deep.
facts: Founded by freed Black Americans; independent since 1847 and never colonized. Its flag looks like the US flag with one star.
Monrovia is named after US President James Monroe.
Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, elected in 2005, was the first elected female head of state in Africa.

cards.shape: Mali is named after the medieval Mali Empire, the realm of Mansa Musa, whose heartland lay along the upper Niger in what is now southern Mali and Guinea. The colony was called French Sudan, and in 1959 it joined Senegal in the Mali Federation, which became independent in June 1960 but split apart two months later; Senegal went its own way and French Sudan kept the name Mali. Its odd bow-tie shape comes from French colonial lines that pushed a big wedge north deep into the Sahara, while the Niger River bends through the middle, past Timbuktu.
facts: Mansa Musa, 14th-century ruler of the Mali Empire, gave away so much gold on his trip to Mecca that its price in Cairo crashed for years.
The Great Mosque of Djenné is the largest mud-brick building in the world.
Families in Timbuktu still keep hundreds of thousands of centuries-old manuscripts.

cards.shape: Mauritania's name echoes Roman Mauretania, the land of the Moors, even though that ancient province lay further north, in today's Morocco and Algeria. Its long straight borders run across empty Sahara, while its southern border follows the Senegal River, and as a colony it had so little in the way of towns that it was run from Saint-Louis in Senegal; the capital, Nouakchott, was built almost from scratch around independence in 1960. Morocco claimed all of Mauritania at first and only recognized it in 1969. When Spain left Western Sahara in 1975-76, Mauritania took its southern third, but it gave the land up in 1979 after a ruinous war with the Polisario independence fighters, and Morocco took it instead.
facts: The Richat Structure, the “Eye of the Sahara”, is a 40 km-wide set of rings visible from space.
Its iron-ore trains are among the longest in the world, over 2 km long.
The last country in the world to abolish slavery, in 1981.

cards.shape: Niger is named after the Niger River, but the river only crosses its far southwest corner, around the capital Niamey; most of the country, the biggest in West Africa, is Sahara. Its southern neighbor Nigeria takes its name from the same river, but they were never one country: France ruled Niger and Britain ruled Nigeria, and their long border was drawn by Anglo-French agreements between 1890 and 1910 that cut through Hausa lands, leaving Hausa people on both sides. The French name is pronounced roughly "nee-ZHAIR", which helps tell it apart from Nigeria.
facts: The Ténéré Tree, once the most isolated tree on Earth, was knocked down by a truck driver in 1973.
Named after the Niger River; about 80% of the country is in the Sahara.
Has one of the youngest populations in the world — the median age is around 15.
Fossils of Nigersaurus, a dinosaur with hundreds of teeth, were found in its desert.

cards.shape: Nigeria takes its name from the Niger River, a name suggested by the British journalist Flora Shaw in 1897; neighboring Niger, a former French colony, is named after the same river. The Niger and its tributary the Benue meet in the middle of the country in a Y, which roughly splits it into the north (mostly Hausa-Fulani), the southwest (Yoruba) and the southeast (Igbo). Britain ran the north and south as separate protectorates until merging them in 1914, and those regional divides fed the civil war of 1967-70, when the southeast tried to break away as Biafra. Its eastern border shifted too: in 1961 the northern part of British Cameroons voted to join Nigeria while the southern part joined Cameroon.
facts: Africa's most populous country, with over 200 million people.
More than 500 languages are spoken in Nigeria.
Nollywood is one of the largest film industries in the world by number of films made.
Abuja was built as a planned capital and replaced Lagos in 1991.

cards.shape: Senegal wraps around the Gambia on three sides, so that thin strip along the Gambia River cuts Senegal's southern region, the Casamance, off from the rest of the country. That comes from the 1800s, when France took the land all around while Britain held on to the river and its trading posts, a line fixed by an 1889 Anglo-French deal. The country is named after the Senegal River, which forms its northern border with Mauritania, and its capital Dakar sits on the Cap-Vert peninsula, the westernmost point of mainland Africa. The two countries tried joining as the Senegambia Confederation from 1982, but it broke up in 1989.
facts: Lake Retba is bright pink, coloured by salt-loving algae.
Home to the westernmost point of mainland Africa, near Dakar.
Gorée Island, off Dakar, is a memorial to the Atlantic slave trade.
For about 30 years the Paris–Dakar Rally finished here.

cards.shape: Sierra Leone is a compact, roundish country that French Guinea wraps around on the north and east, with Liberia to the southeast. The name is Portuguese, from the 1460s, meaning "lion mountains" for the hills behind the harbor, though why lions is not known. Its modern story starts in 1787, when British abolitionists founded a settlement there for freed slaves, later Freetown, and Britain only claimed the inland territory as a protectorate in 1896, by which time France held everything around it, which is why it stayed small.
facts: The Cotton Tree, a giant tree in central Freetown, was the city's symbol for over 200 years until a storm toppled it in 2023.
Freetown was founded in 1792 as a settlement for freed slaves.
The name comes from Portuguese “Serra Leoa” — lion mountains.

cards.shape: Togo is a narrow strip, only about 56 km of coast, stretching nearly 580 km inland between Ghana and Benin. It is the eastern part of the old German colony of Togoland, which Britain and France seized in 1914 and split between them; the British western part joined Ghana after a 1956 vote, and the French part became independent Togo in 1960. The split cut through the Ewe people, who live on both sides of the Togo-Ghana border. The name comes from the lakeside town now called Togoville where the German explorer Gustav Nachtigal signed a treaty in 1884.
facts: Togo is very narrow: under 100 km wide but more than 500 km long, with only about 56 km of coast.
Lomé's Akodésséwa fetish market sells ingredients for traditional Vodun remedies.
In Koutammakou, the Batammariba people build two-storey mud tower-houses, a UNESCO site.

cards.shape: The little piece of Angola floating north of the rest, Cabinda, is cut off by the DRC's narrow corridor to the sea along the Congo River's mouth, which King Leopold II's Congo Free State won in the 1880s. Cabinda had signed its own protection treaty with Portugal in 1885 and was only run as part of Angola later, which is why a separatist movement there still argues it's a separate country; today it produces much of Angola's oil. The name Angola comes from ngola, the title of the kings of Ndongo, the kingdom the Portuguese fought and traded with around Luanda from the 1500s.
facts: The giant sable antelope, feared wiped out by the civil war, was rediscovered by camera traps in the 2000s.
Its province of Cabinda is cut off from the rest of the country by a strip of the DR Congo.
One of Africa's biggest oil producers; a Portuguese colony until 1975.

cards.shape: Cameroon is shaped like a triangle with a long tail running north up to Lake Chad, and its name comes from Portuguese sailors of the 1470s, who called the Wouri River estuary the Rio dos Camarões, the River of Shrimp. It became the German colony of Kamerun in 1884, and the Germans pushed it north to reach Lake Chad. After World War I it was split: France got most of it, Britain got two strips along the Nigerian border. In 1961 votes the southern British strip chose to join Cameroon and the northern one chose Nigeria, which is why Cameroon has an English-speaking region in the west and the border there looks so jagged.
facts: In 1986 Lake Nyos suddenly released a cloud of carbon dioxide that suffocated about 1,700 people.
Called “Africa in miniature” for having beaches, desert, mountains, savanna and rainforest.
The name comes from Portuguese “Rio dos Camarões” — river of prawns.
Mount Cameroon (4,040 m) is an active volcano and the highest peak in West and Central Africa.

cards.shape: The Central African Republic's name is just a description of where it is, and it replaced the colonial name Ubangi-Shari, after its two main rivers: the Ubangi, which forms most of its southern border with the DRC, and the Chari, which rises in the north and flows on to Lake Chad. The plain name was chosen by independence leader Barthélemy Boganda, who hoped to build a big united state out of all of French Equatorial Africa. When the other colonies (Chad, Gabon and the Republic of the Congo) chose to go their own way in late 1958, the name stuck to this one landlocked territory alone. For a few years, 1976 to 1979, it was renamed the Central African Empire under self-crowned emperor Jean-Bédel Bokassa.
facts: In 1977 its leader Jean-Bédel Bokassa crowned himself emperor in a ceremony costing about a third of the national budget.
Landlocked near the geographic centre of the continent.
In Dzanga-Sangha, hundreds of forest elephants gather in a single forest clearing.

cards.shape: Chad is named after Lake Chad, in its far west, where it meets Niger, Nigeria and Cameroon; the lake has shrunk dramatically since the 1960s, by most estimates about 90%. It was the northern end of French Equatorial Africa, and its long northern border with Libya cuts straight across the Sahara. A strip along that border, the Aouzou Strip, was promised to Italian Libya in a 1935 Franco-Italian deal that was never ratified, and Libya under Gaddafi occupied it in 1973. Chad pushed Libya back in fighting in 1987, and after the International Court of Justice ruled in 1994 that the strip belongs to Chad, Libya withdrew.
facts: The Bodélé Depression is the biggest dust source on Earth — its dust blows across the Atlantic and helps fertilize the Amazon.
Named after Lake Chad, which has shrunk by about 90% since the 1960s.
“Toumaï”, a 7-million-year-old skull found here, is one of the oldest known human relatives.
Emi Koussi, in the Tibesti Mountains, is the highest point in the Sahara.

cards.shape: This is the smaller Congo, sitting west and north of the Congo River, and the river is where it and the much bigger Democratic Republic of the Congo split. In the 1880s the Italian-born French explorer Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza signed treaties on this side of the river while Henry Morton Stanley claimed the other side for Belgium's King Leopold II, so the river became the line between French Congo and Leopold's Congo Free State (later the Belgian Congo). Both kept the river's name at independence in 1960, which is why there are two Congos; they were never one country, and their capitals, Brazzaville (named after de Brazza) and Kinshasa, face each other across the river.
facts: Brazzaville and Kinshasa face each other across the Congo River — the closest pair of capital cities apart from Rome and Vatican City.
Brazzaville is named after the explorer Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza, who is buried there.
Roughly two-thirds of the country is covered by rainforest.
Odzala-Kokoua, founded in 1935, is one of Africa's oldest national parks and a gorilla stronghold.

cards.shape: The DRC is huge, the second-largest country in Africa and about seven times the size of the Republic of the Congo across the river, yet it touches the ocean through only a sliver of coast, roughly 40 km, at the Congo River's mouth. It started as the Congo Free State, King Leopold II of Belgium's personal colony, drawn in the 1880s to take in most of the Congo River basin, plus a corridor to the sea between Portuguese lands, which is why Angola's Cabinda province is cut off from the rest of Angola. The two Congos share the river's name but were never one country: France took the land north and west of the river, Leopold the rest. The DRC was called Zaire from 1971 to 1997.
facts: Bonobos — with chimpanzees, our closest living relatives — live in the wild only here.
The Congo River is the deepest river in the world, over 220 m in places.
Produces about 70% of the world's cobalt, used in phone and car batteries.
The second-largest country in Africa by area.
Kinshasa is the largest French-speaking city in the world.

cards.shape: Equatorial Guinea comes in pieces: a small square of mainland, Río Muni, between Cameroon and Gabon, plus the island of Bioko up off the Cameroon coast, where the capital Malabo is, and tiny Annobón far to the south past São Tomé. Spain got the islands from Portugal in 1778 in exchange for land in South America, mainly hoping for a slave-trading base, and only had its mainland strip confirmed by France in 1900, much smaller than it had claimed. That is why it is the only Spanish-speaking country in sub-Saharan Africa. Despite the name, most of it lies just north of the equator; only Annobón is south of it.
facts: Despite its name, almost none of it is on the Equator — only its tiny island of Annobón lies south of it.
The only African country where Spanish is an official language.
Its capital, Malabo, is on Bioko Island, not on the mainland.

cards.shape: Gabon's name comes from the Portuguese word gabão, a hooded cloak, which sailors in the 1400s thought the Komo River estuary looked like. That estuary is where its capital, Libreville ("free town"), was founded by the French in 1849 with Africans freed from a captured slave ship. The country sits right on the equator and mostly covers the basin of one river, the Ogooué. The ruler-straight lines cutting off its northwest corner mark Equatorial Guinea's mainland, Río Muni, a small piece of coast Spain held onto between French Gabon and German Kamerun.
facts: About 2 billion years ago, natural nuclear reactors ran underground at Oklo — the only ones ever found on Earth.
Almost 90% of Gabon is forest.
In Loango National Park, elephants and hippos walk on the beach.

cards.shape: São Tomé and Príncipe is two small volcanic islands in the Gulf of Guinea, part of the same chain of volcanoes as Equatorial Guinea's Bioko island and Mount Cameroon, and it's the second-smallest country in Africa after the Seychelles. The islands were uninhabited when Portuguese sailors arrived around 1470, and São Tomé is named for Saint Thomas, on whose feast day it was reportedly sighted. Príncipe, the "Prince's island," was renamed in honor of the Portuguese crown prince. Portugal turned the islands into sugar and later cocoa plantations worked by enslaved and forced labor brought from mainland Africa, and ruled them until independence in 1975.
facts: Pico Cão Grande is a needle of volcanic rock rising over 300 m straight out of the jungle.
Africa's second-smallest country; the Equator runs right across its islet Ilhéu das Rolas.
Around 1908 it was the world's largest cocoa producer.

cards.shape: Burundi is a small, densely packed country at the northeast end of Lake Tanganyika, and it looks like a twin of Rwanda, just to its north, because it nearly is one. Both were old kingdoms in the highlands long before colonial rule, both were in German East Africa, and after World War I Belgium ran them together as Ruanda-Urundi while Britain took the rest, Tanganyika, so they ended up separate from Tanzania. At independence in 1962 they became two countries, following the old kingdom boundaries, and they share very similar languages and a similar Hutu and Tutsi population mix.
facts: One of the claimed southernmost sources of the Nile is a spring in Burundi, marked with a small pyramid.
Lies on Lake Tanganyika, the world's second-deepest lake.
The Royal Drummers of Burundi are a UNESCO-listed tradition.

cards.shape: Comoros is a chain of volcanic islands between Madagascar and Mozambique, but maps show only three of the four main islands as Comoros. When France held referendums in 1974, Grande Comore, Anjouan and Mohéli voted for independence while Mayotte, the island nearest Madagascar, voted to stay French; Comoros declared independence in 1975 and still claims Mayotte, which became a full French department in 2011. In 1997 Anjouan and Mohéli tried to break away too, and Anjouan even asked to return to French rule, until a new constitution in 2001 gave each island more self-rule. The name comes from the Arabic for 'islands of the moon'.
facts: The coelacanth, a fish thought extinct for 66 million years, was found alive in its waters.
A leading producer of ylang-ylang, a flower oil used in perfumes.
Mount Karthala, on the main island, is an active volcano that last erupted in 2007.
A fourth island, Mayotte, voted to stay French — Comoros still claims it.

cards.shape: Djibouti is a tiny wedge wrapped around the Gulf of Tadjoura, right where the Red Sea opens into the Gulf of Aden at the Bab-el-Mandeb strait. France bought a foothold at Obock in 1862 and built the port of Djibouti in the 1880s-90s as a coaling station on the route to Suez and its colonies further east, then a railway to Addis Ababa, so the colony (French Somaliland) was drawn around a port and its hinterland rather than around any people. Its two main groups, the Afar in the north and the Somali Issa in the south, gave it the name French Territory of the Afars and the Issas from 1967, and at independence in 1977 it took the capital's name. Since the 1998-2000 war with Eritrea closed Ethiopia's route to the Eritrean port of Assab, most of Ethiopia's trade goes through Djibouti, and its strategic spot also makes it host to US, French and Chinese military bases.
facts: Africa is slowly splitting apart here, where three tectonic plates pull away from each other.
Lake Assal, 155 m below sea level, is the lowest point in Africa — and one of the saltiest lakes on Earth.
Guarding the entrance to the Red Sea, it hosts military bases of the US, France, China, Japan and others.

cards.shape: Eritrea is a long, thin strip along the Red Sea coast, and that strip is exactly what Ethiopia lost. Italy took the coast in 1890 and named its new colony after the sea itself, from the Greek name for the Red Sea, Erythra Thalassa. After World War II the UN federated Eritrea with Ethiopia in 1952, Ethiopia annexed it outright in 1962, and after a 30-year war Eritrea became independent in 1993, leaving Ethiopia landlocked behind it. The two then fought a bloody border war in 1998-2000 over a few disputed towns along that inland frontier.
facts: Asmara's Fiat Tagliero building, from 1938, is a petrol station shaped like an aeroplane.
Asmara's Italian-era modernist architecture is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Became independent from Ethiopia in 1993 after a 30-year war.
The Danakil Depression, shared with Ethiopia, is one of the hottest places on Earth.

cards.shape: Ethiopia has no coast, but it did have one for about forty years. Italy took the Red Sea coast, long held by the Ottomans and then Egypt, as its colony Eritrea in 1890, and when Ethiopia beat Italy at Adwa in 1896 it stayed independent but the coast stayed Italian. After World War II the UN joined Eritrea to Ethiopia in a federation in 1952, Ethiopia annexed it outright in 1962, and a 30-year war ended with Eritrea independent in 1993, leaving Ethiopia the most populous landlocked country in the world, now shipping mostly through Djibouti. Its big bulge east into the Horn, the Ogaden, comes from Emperor Menelik II's expansion in the late 1800s and is Somali-inhabited, which is why Somalia fought Ethiopia over it in 1977-78.
facts: Uses its own calendar: 13 months, and about 7–8 years behind the Gregorian one.
Coffee was first discovered here — legend credits a goat herder named Kaldi.
Lucy, a 3.2-million-year-old human ancestor, was found here in 1974.
Lalibela's churches were carved downward into solid rock in the 12th–13th centuries.
Never colonized, apart from a brief Italian occupation (1936–41). The African Union is headquartered in Addis Ababa.

cards.shape: Kenya is named after Mount Kenya, its highest peak, while Africa's highest, Kilimanjaro, sits just over the border in Tanzania where the otherwise straight line from the coast to Lake Victoria takes a bend. That line was an 1886 Anglo-German split of East Africa into British and German spheres, and the bend put Kilimanjaro, where Germans had signed treaties, on the German side. (The story that Queen Victoria gave the mountain to her grandson, the future Kaiser Wilhelm II, as a birthday present is a legend.) Kenya's boundary with Somalia also moved: in 1924-25 Britain handed the strip of land west of the Juba River, Jubaland, to Italian Somaliland as a reward for Italy joining the Allies in World War I.
facts: Kenyan men won the Olympic steeplechase at every Games they took part in from 1968 to 2016.
Each year over a million wildebeest migrate through the Maasai Mara.
Nairobi National Park has lions and rhinos with the city skyline in view.
Lake Turkana is the world's largest permanent desert lake.

cards.shape: Madagascar is the world's fourth-largest island, about 1,600 km long, and it sits off Africa because it broke away from it, together with India, roughly 160 million years ago, then split from India around 90 million years ago. That long isolation is why most of its plants and animals, like lemurs, live nowhere else. Its people are isolated from Africa in their own way: the first big settlement came by sea from what is now Indonesia, around 1,500 years ago, and Malagasy is closest to a language spoken on Borneo, with African influence added later. The name probably comes from Marco Polo, who wrote about 'Madeigascar' but seems to have mixed it up with Mogadishu in Somalia.
facts: Its first settlers sailed from Borneo about 1,500 years ago — Malagasy is related to languages of Indonesia.
About 90% of its wildlife exists nowhere else — including every species of lemur.
The world's fourth-largest island.

cards.shape: Malawi is a long, thin country, roughly 900 km from north to south but in places under 100 km wide, because it is wrapped around the western shore of Lake Malawi, which covers about a fifth of its area. Britain claimed it in 1891 as the British Central Africa Protectorate (renamed Nyasaland in 1907), following the Scottish missionaries who came after David Livingstone, and Portugal's Mozambique took the land on the far shore. The border with Tanzania runs along the lake's northeastern shoreline rather than down the middle, following an 1890 Anglo-German treaty, so Malawi claims the whole northern lake and Tanzania still disputes it. On the Mozambique side, two small islands, Likoma and Chizumulu, are Malawian enclaves sitting in Mozambique's part of the lake, because they were the base of an Anglican mission when the line was drawn.
facts: Lake Malawi has more fish species than any other lake on Earth — hundreds of kinds of cichlid.
Lake Malawi covers about a fifth of the country.
Known as “the warm heart of Africa”.

cards.shape: Mauritius was uninhabited until Europeans arrived, which is why it has a European name: the Dutch named it in 1598 after Prince Maurice of Nassau, then France ran it as Île de France until Britain took it in 1810. The country is more than the main island, also taking in Rodrigues about 560 km east and other scattered islands. In 1965, just before independence, Britain split off the Chagos Islands, removed their people and let the US build a base on Diego Garcia; Mauritius kept claiming them, the UN's top court backed it in 2019, and Britain signed a treaty in 2025 to hand them over while keeping the base on a long lease.
facts: The only home of the dodo, extinct by the late 1600s.
The “underwater waterfall” off Le Morne is an illusion made by sand sliding into deep water.
Nobody lived on Mauritius until the Dutch settled it in 1638.

cards.shape: Mozambique is a long strip of coast, about 2,500 km of it, with a wedge pushing far inland along the Zambezi River between Zambia, Zimbabwe and Malawi. The Portuguese held trading posts on this coast from the early 1500s and old river towns like Tete up the Zambezi, which is why that wedge exists, but their 1880s 'Pink Map' plan to join Mozambique to Angola across the continent was stopped by a British ultimatum in 1890, and Britain took the land in between. The country is named after the small Island of Mozambique, the old Portuguese capital, whose name is said to come from an Arab sheikh, Mussa Bin Bique. Because it ended up almost surrounded by former British colonies, it joined the Commonwealth in 1995, the first member that was never ruled by Britain.
facts: Its flag is the only national flag featuring a modern rifle (an AK-47).
Ilha de Moçambique, a small coral island, was the colonial capital for centuries and gave the country its name.
Has about 2,500 km of Indian Ocean coastline.

cards.shape: Rwanda is one of Africa's smallest countries and the most densely populated on the mainland, and it sits next to Burundi, which is almost the same size and shape. Both were old kingdoms in the hills between Lake Victoria and the western lakes long before Europeans arrived, which is why they kept separate identities. Germany ruled them as part of German East Africa, and after World War I Belgium took them over together as Ruanda-Urundi while Britain got the rest as Tanganyika, which is why they never became part of Tanzania. They split into two countries at independence in 1962, roughly along the old kingdom lines, with Lake Kivu forming much of Rwanda's western border with the DRC.
facts: Women hold over 60% of seats in parliament — the highest share in the world.
Known as the “land of a thousand hills”.
Plastic bags are banned, and on the last Saturday of each month everyone does community work (Umuganda).
Home to mountain gorillas in Volcanoes National Park.

cards.shape: Seychelles is Africa's smallest country, about 115 islands with less land than a large city, scattered across the Indian Ocean northeast of Madagascar. Its main islands are unusual: they are granite, a scrap of continent that broke away from Madagascar along with India and was left behind about 66 million years ago when India drifted north, while most of the rest are low coral atolls. France claimed the islands in 1756 and named them after Jean Moreau de Séchelles, Louis XV's finance minister; Britain took them in 1814 and ran them from Mauritius until 1903. In 1965 Britain also detached three of its outer island groups along with Mauritius's Chagos Islands into a new British territory, but gave the Seychelles ones back at independence in 1976.
facts: Aldabra Atoll is home to about 100,000 giant tortoises.
The coco de mer palm grows the largest seed in the plant kingdom.
Africa's smallest country by population, about 100,000 people on 115 islands.
Nobody lived here until French settlers arrived in 1770.

cards.shape: Somalia wraps around the tip of the Horn of Africa like a figure 7, giving it the longest coastline of any country on mainland Africa, over 3,000 km. It was made in 1960 by joining two colonies: British Somaliland along the Gulf of Aden in the north and Italian Somaliland down the Indian Ocean coast. Many Somalis were left outside it, in Djibouti, Ethiopia's Ogaden and northeastern Kenya, which is what the five-pointed star on the flag stands for and why Somalia fought Ethiopia over the Ogaden in 1977-78. Since 1991 the old British part has run itself as Somaliland, a self-declared country that only Israel recognizes, since December 2025.
facts: Has the longest coastline of any country on mainland Africa, around 3,000 km.
Somalia has been called “a nation of poets” for its strong oral poetry tradition.
The cave paintings of Laas Geel, thousands of years old, are among the best preserved in Africa.
Somaliland, in the north-west, has governed itself since 1991 but isn't internationally recognised.

cards.shape: South Sudan is literally the south of Sudan: it became independent in 2011, which makes it the world's newest country, and Sudan to its north is still about three times its size. Under British rule Sudan's mostly Arabic-speaking Muslim north and the largely Christian and traditional-religion south were governed almost separately, but they were handed over as one country in 1956, and the south fought two long civil wars against the north before a 2005 peace deal led to a referendum where nearly everyone voted to leave. It is landlocked and most of its oil still has to reach the sea by pipeline through Sudan to Port Sudan, and parts of the border with Sudan, notably the Abyei area, are still disputed. At its southeast corner, maps differ over the Ilemi Triangle, a patch claimed by South Sudan but run by Kenya.
facts: The world's newest widely recognized country, independent from Sudan since 2011.
Millions of antelope migrate across it each year — one of the largest land migrations on Earth.
The Sudd is one of the largest wetlands in the world.

cards.shape: Tanzania's name is a mashup of its two parts: mainland Tanganyika and the islands of Zanzibar, which merged in 1964, a few months after a revolution overthrew Zanzibar's sultan. Tanganyika was named after the lake on its western border, and the country's edges are mostly water: Lake Victoria in the north, Lake Tanganyika in the west and Lake Malawi (Lake Nyasa) in the southwest, where Malawi still claims the lake's waters right up to the Tanzanian shore. The mainland is the former German East Africa minus Rwanda and Burundi, which went to Belgium after World War I. The straight border with Kenya, with its bend around Kilimanjaro, comes from an 1886 Anglo-German deal that split East Africa between them.
facts: Freddie Mercury, of Queen, was born in Zanzibar.
Mount Kilimanjaro (5,895 m) is the highest mountain in Africa.
Olduvai Gorge has stone tools and fossils of human ancestors going back about 2 million years.
Includes the island of Zanzibar, once a hub of the spice trade.

cards.shape: Uganda takes its name from Buganda, the powerful kingdom on the north shore of Lake Victoria that Britain made the core of its protectorate in the 1890s, using the Swahili form of the name. Much of its border runs through lakes: it shares Lake Victoria with Kenya and Tanzania, with the southern line running straight across the water along 1 degree south, and it splits Lakes Albert and Edward with the DRC to the west. It used to be bigger to the east: in 1902 Britain moved its Eastern Province, including what is now western Kenya around Kisumu, to the Kenya side so the new Uganda Railway from Mombasa would sit under one administration.
facts: The Rwenzori — the “Mountains of the Moon” — have glaciers almost on the Equator.
The White Nile leaves Lake Victoria at Jinja.
Bwindi Forest is home to about half of the world's mountain gorillas.

cards.shape: Zambia has an odd, pinched butterfly shape, nearly cut in two by the Congo Pedicle, a thick finger of the DRC's copper-rich Katanga region that pokes down into it. That line comes from 1890s deals between Britain and Belgian King Leopold II's Congo Free State, each racing to grab the mineral country, with Britain's share run by Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company and joined up as Northern Rhodesia in 1911. At independence in 1964 it dropped Rhodes's name and took one from the Zambezi River, which forms its southern border with Zimbabwe, the former Southern Rhodesia. In the southwest it touches Botswana for only about 150 m at Kazungula, one of the shortest borders in the world, now crossed by a bridge.
facts: In the dry season you can swim in Devil's Pool, right at the edge of Victoria Falls.
Shares Victoria Falls — “Mosi-oa-Tunya”, the smoke that thunders — with Zimbabwe.
Each November about 10 million fruit bats gather in Kasanka National Park.
One of the world's biggest copper producers.

cards.shape: Zimbabwe sits between two rivers: the Zambezi, with Victoria Falls and the huge Lake Kariba, forms its northern border with Zambia, and the Limpopo its southern border with South Africa. Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company took it from 1890, and it became Southern Rhodesia, with Zambia to the north as Northern Rhodesia, and the two were joined with Malawi in a federation from 1953 to 1963. When its white minority government declared independence alone in 1965 as Rhodesia, the river became a hostile frontier, and only after a long war did the country become independent under majority rule in 1980. It took its new name from Great Zimbabwe, the medieval stone city in its southeast whose ruins colonial authorities had claimed could not have been built by Africans; the name is usually translated from Shona as 'houses of stone'.
facts: In 2008 inflation was so high it printed a 100-trillion-dollar note.
Named after Great Zimbabwe, a stone city built between the 11th and 15th centuries.
The Zimbabwe Bird, a soapstone carving found at Great Zimbabwe, is on its flag.
Lake Kariba, shared with Zambia, is the largest artificial reservoir in the world by volume.

cards.shape: Botswana means "land of the Tswana," but more Tswana people actually live across the border in South Africa than in Botswana itself. Britain declared the Bechuanaland Protectorate in 1885 mainly to keep a road north from the Cape open and to stop the Boer republics from joining up with German South West Africa (now Namibia). It was such an afterthought that it was run from Mafeking, a town in South Africa outside its own borders, until the new capital Gaborone was built just before independence in 1966. At its northern tip it touches Zambia along a border only about 150 meters long, at Kazungula on the Zambezi, squeezed between Namibia's Caprivi Strip and Zimbabwe.
facts: The Okavango Delta is a river delta that never reaches the sea — it drains into the Kalahari.
Has the largest elephant population in the world, around 130,000.
The 1,111-carat Lesedi La Rona, one of the largest diamonds ever found, was dug up here in 2015.
The Makgadikgadi Pans are among the largest salt flats in the world.

cards.shape: Eswatini is almost surrounded by South Africa, but unlike Lesotho it also touches Mozambique on its east side. It is named after the 1800s king Mswati II, whose people became known as the Swazi; King Mswati III changed the official name from Swaziland to Eswatini, "land of the Swazi" in the Swazi language, in 2018. The kingdom lost land to the Boer Transvaal in border deals of the 1880s, so many Swazi live in South Africa today. After the Boer War it was a British protectorate, stayed out of South Africa when that country formed in 1910, and became independent in 1968.
facts: One of the last absolute monarchies in the world.
Renamed from Swaziland to Eswatini in 2018.
Each year tens of thousands of young women take part in the Umhlanga, or Reed Dance.
Ngwenya Mine is one of the oldest known mines, dug for red ochre over 40,000 years ago.

cards.shape: Lesotho is completely surrounded by South Africa, one of only three countries in the world entirely inside another (with Vatican City and San Marino). In the mid-1800s King Moshoeshoe I's Basotho held out in the mountains against the Boers of the Orange Free State, but lost their fertile western lowlands, so he asked Britain for protection and Basutoland became a British protectorate in 1868. When South Africa was formed in 1910, Basutoland stayed under British rule instead of joining it, and became independent as Lesotho in 1966. That mountain refuge is why the whole country is high ground: its lowest point is about 1,400 m, the highest low point of any country.
facts: The whole country is above 1,400 m — the highest “lowest point” of any country.
Completely surrounded by South Africa.
Maletsunyane Falls drops nearly 200 m in a single plunge.
Has one of the few ski resorts in Africa.

cards.shape: The long, thin finger poking east from Namibia's northeast corner is the Caprivi Strip, about 450 km long. Germany, which ruled the territory as German South West Africa, got it from Britain in an 1890 treaty and named it after its chancellor, Leo von Caprivi, hoping to reach the Zambezi River and a route toward its East African colony, but the Zambezi turned out to be unnavigable, not least because of Victoria Falls downstream. The country is named after the Namib Desert along its coast, and the port of Walvis Bay in the middle of that coast was a separate British (later South African) enclave that South Africa only handed over in 1994, four years after Namibia's independence.
facts: The Hoba meteorite, the largest known, weighs about 60 tonnes and still lies where it fell.
The Namib is thought to be the world's oldest desert, with some of the tallest sand dunes.
The Skeleton Coast is named for the whale bones and shipwrecks along it.
The first country to write environmental protection into its constitution.

cards.shape: South Africa has a hole in it: Lesotho sits completely inside it, and Eswatini is nearly inside it too. The country formed in 1910 as the Union of South Africa by joining four British colonies, two of them the former Boer republics of the Transvaal and the Orange Free State, and its plain descriptive name dates from then. Britain kept Basutoland (Lesotho), Swaziland (Eswatini) and Bechuanaland (Botswana) out, ruling them directly, and kept refusing South Africa's demands to hand them over, all the more firmly once apartheid began, so all three became separate countries in the 1960s. It also held the port of Walvis Bay in the middle of Namibia's coast until 1994.
facts: Two Nobel Peace Prize winners, Nelson Mandela and Desmond Tutu, lived on the same street in Soweto.
Has three capitals: Pretoria (executive), Cape Town (parliament) and Bloemfontein (courts).
Has 12 official languages, including South African Sign Language.
Mponeng gold mine is the deepest mine in the world, about 4 km down.
Table Mountain has more plant species than the whole of the UK.
